classification.difficultyReason: Carry out three specified substitutions, transform the limits and simplify the trigonometric integrand; agreement follows directly from the three evaluations.

content.prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\,dx$ using three different methods and confirm you get the same answer.

answer.worked:
Let $u=1+x^2$, so $du=2x\,dx$ and $dx=\dfrac{du}{2x}$.

Limits: when $x=0$, $u=1$; when $x=1$, $u=2$.

$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^1\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\,dx&=\frac12\int_1^2u^{-1/2}\,du\\&=\frac12\left[2\sqrt u\right]_1^2\\&=\left[\sqrt u\right]_1^2\\&=\sqrt2-1.\end{aligned}$$

Let $x^2=t$, so $x=\sqrt t$ and $dx=\dfrac{dt}{2\sqrt t}$.

Limits: when $x=0$, $t=0$; when $x=1$, $t=1$.

$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^1\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\,dx&=\int_0^1\left(\frac{\sqrt t}{\sqrt{1+t}}\cdot\frac1{2\sqrt t}\right)\,dt\\&=\frac12\int_0^1(1+t)^{-1/2}\,dt\\&=\frac12\left[2\sqrt{1+t}\right]_0^1\\&=\left[\sqrt{1+t}\right]_0^1\\&=\sqrt2-1.\end{aligned}$$

Let $x=\tan\theta$, so $dx=\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$ and $\sqrt{1+x^2}=\sec\theta$ on $0\leq\theta\leq\dfrac\pi4$.

Limits: when $x=0$, $\theta=0$; when $x=1$, $\theta=\dfrac\pi4$.

$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^1\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\,dx&=\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{\tan\theta}{\sec\theta}\sec^2\theta\,d\theta\\&=\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos^2\theta}\,d\theta\\&=\int_0^{\pi/4}\sin\theta(\cos\theta)^{-2}\,d\theta\\&=\left[(\cos\theta)^{-1}\right]_0^{\pi/4}\\&=\frac1{\cos(\pi/4)}-\frac1{\cos0}\\&=\sqrt2-1.\end{aligned}$$

All three methods give $\sqrt2-1$.
